Lower the barrier. Keep the bar.

Week 14 · Chapters 4 and 5 · Intelligence, individual differences and exceptionalities

Study · Week 14

Read Chapters 4 and 5 of the textbook (Eggen & Kauchak, 2025) first, then this. Chapter 4 covers culture, language and income. Chapter 5 covers intelligence, ability grouping and learners with exceptionalities. This week asks one question of all of it: when a student struggles, do you change the barrier or the bar?

About 40 minutes: reading, two places you stop and write, and eight quick checks.

Start with the file

You read a district file this week. Seventeen students. Two were evaluated because a parent asked, and both parents knew exactly what to ask for. One referral died on a consent form nobody chased. A screening tool now learns from that record.

Keep the file open. Every idea in this brief comes back to it.

Here is the question that runs through the week. When a student struggles, what do you change? You can change the barrier: the thing that stands between the student and the learning. Or you can change the bar: what the student is expected to learn. Most new teachers reach for the bar. It feels kind. It is usually the wrong move.

What intelligence is

Chapter 5 defines intelligence as the ability to acquire knowledge, to think and reason in the abstract, and to solve problems. Psychologists have argued for a century about whether that is one ability or many.

One general ability Charles Spearman (1904) noticed that people who do well on one kind of mental test tend to do well on the others. He called the shared part g, general intelligence. Most modern IQ tests report a total score built on that idea.

Broad and narrow abilities The Cattell–Horn–Carroll model (McGrew, 2009) keeps g at the top and adds broad abilities under it: reasoning with new problems, stored knowledge, processing speed, working memory, visual and auditory processing. Most school psychologists read test results through this model.

Multiple intelligences Howard Gardner (1983) proposed separate intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalist. Teachers love the theory. The research support is weak, because the intelligences overlap more than the theory predicts. Its lasting use is a reminder: school rewards two or three of them and ignores the rest.

Successful intelligence Robert Sternberg (1985) describes three abilities: analytical (solve the problem on the page), creative (deal with a new problem) and practical (adapt to the world you live in). A student can be low on the first and high on the other two. Most tests only see the first.

Adaptive intelligence Sternberg’s newer question (Sternberg, 2021): intelligent for what? He points to a paradox. IQ scores rose for a century, and the world’s big problems, from climate change to pandemics, did not shrink. Tests reward solving someone else’s problem fast. Adaptive intelligence is using your abilities to solve real problems for the common good, over the long run as well as today. It counts what a student does with the score.

What IQ predicts. It predicts school grades well (Deary et al., 2007). It predicts how long people stay in school and, more weakly, success at work. It is one of the strongest single predictors psychology has.

What IQ does not fix. Intelligence grows with schooling. A review of natural experiments found that each extra year of education raises IQ by one to five points (Ritchie & Tucker-Drob, 2018). Average scores also rose about three points per decade across the 20th century, the Flynn effect (Flynn, 1987). Genes did not change that fast. Schools, nutrition and the mental demands of daily life did.

And now some scores are falling. In Norway, scores of young men born after about 1975 started dropping. The drop shows up between brothers in the same family, so genes and family background can’t explain it: something in the environment changed (Bratsberg & Rogeberg, 2018). A large U.S. online sample found declines from 2006 to 2018 in verbal reasoning and matrix problems, with a gain in spatial reasoning (Dworak et al., 2023). Nobody knows the cause yet. Changes in schooling, reading habits, screens and tests themselves are all on the list. The lesson is the same in both directions: the environment moves the score, and the environment now includes the tools students think with. Whether offloading thinking to tools is part of the cause is still an open question. It is a fair one to ask.

A test score describes what a student can do today, under these conditions. It does not set a ceiling. The environment you build is part of the score.

True or false?

IQ is fixed at birth, so a teacher can use it to predict what a student will ever be able to learn.

Not quite Schooling raises IQ, and whole countries gained about three points a decade in the 20th century. A score is a snapshot of today, under today’s conditions.

Right IQ predicts school performance, and it also changes. Each year of schooling raises it a little, and the Flynn effect shows how much the environment matters.

Ability grouping, and a claim that fails

Chapter 5 describes ability grouping: placing students with similar scores together. Between-class grouping (tracking) has a cost. Students in low tracks get less challenging work, less experienced teachers, and lower expectations. Few of them ever move up. Flexible grouping within a class works better: groups formed for one skill, for a few weeks, then mixed again.

Chapter 5 also takes on learning styles: the claim that a “visual learner” learns better from pictures and an “auditory learner” from talk. Students like the idea. When researchers test it properly, matching teaching to a preferred style does not improve learning (Pashler et al., 2008). Content decides the format. Maps are visual for every learner. Pronunciation is auditory for every learner.

Check yourself

A colleague says, “Darius is a kinesthetic learner, so I let him skip the readings and do the hands-on station instead.” What does Chapter 5 say?

The evidence says no Studies that test style matching properly find no benefit (Pashler et al., 2008). Darius just lost the reading.

Yes Two problems at once. The style claim fails when tested, and the “fix” removes a task his peers still do. That lowers the bar for him.

No test fixes it A preference you can measure still doesn’t predict who learns better from which format.

No An accommodation comes from a documented need in an IEP or 504 plan. A style label creates no legal right, and nothing here removes a barrier.

Talent is developed

Intelligence is where the story starts. Talent is what a person builds with it over years, in a domain, with teaching, practice and opportunity. Subotnik et al. (2011) describe talent development in four claims:

  1. Abilities matter, and they can grow.
  2. Each domain has its own path. Math talent shows early. Talent in history or psychology often shows late.
  3. Opportunity has to be offered, and taken.
  4. Psychosocial skills decide a lot: persistence, coping with criticism, belief in your own growth.

Schools are not the only place that tries to find and grow talent. Sports teams scout athletes. Companies pick and train future leaders. Jonathan Wai and I mapped 80 years of talent identification research across these fields (Parra-Martinez & Wai, 2023). Each field solves the same problem: who has potential, where to invest, and when to check again. The fields rarely read each other.

Sport teaches one thing schools often forget. A good scout does not test a child once at age eight and close the door. Scouts watch players again every season. A late bloomer gets another look.

In a paper Ophélie Desmet and I just published, we call this cycle talent management (Parra-Martinez & Desmet, 2026): identify, offer opportunity and support, watch how the student responds, then revise. It never stops at one score. It checks strengths and needs together. And it uses more than achievement data: motivation, well-being and the student’s own account count too.

Look at your district file again. The record is a gate. Tanya and D’Andre went through it because a parent pushed. Matthew stopped at a consent form. Nobody looked again.

An asset-based teacher starts from what a student can do, then removes what blocks the rest. A deficit-based teacher starts from the gap and builds the whole plan around it.

Intelligence when AI is in the room

Every student you teach will have AI in their pocket. That changes what intelligence looks like in your classroom. It also changes what you can learn from a student’s work.

In the same paper, Desmet and I name three things that can happen when a learner works with AI (Parra-Martinez & Desmet, 2026).

Offloading Using a tool to reduce the mental work of a task (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). A calculator offloads arithmetic. Offloading is a choice about where the thinking happens. An expert who offloads a routine step saves effort for the hard part. A learner who offloads the step they are supposed to be learning loses the practice.

Surrender Accepting the tool’s output without checking it (Shaw & Nave, 2026). The student asks AI to do the work, then copies the result. The product looks fine. The understanding is missing, and confidence goes up anyway.

Augmentation The learner’s judgment and the tool’s capability together produce work neither could produce alone, and the learner grows. The learner can explain the work, catch the tool’s errors, and do better next time.

The strongest evidence so far comes from a randomized trial in Turkish high schools (Bastani et al., 2025). Students who practiced math with unrestricted GPT-4 did 48% better on practice problems. On the exam, without the tool, they did 17% worse than students who never had it. A version that only gave teacher-designed hints improved practice without that loss.

The tool was the same. The design decided whether students offloaded the learning or kept it.

What this means for your subject. AI recalls facts on demand. It cannot decide what matters for your student, check its own answer, or answer for the consequences. Those are thinking skills: framing a problem, weighing evidence, catching an error, defending a choice. Sternberg’s adaptive intelligence asks one more: deciding whether the work is worth doing, and for whom. They are worth more every year. Recall for its own sake is worth less. One warning from Week 7: judgment runs on knowledge. A student who knows nothing about the Civil War cannot catch an AI’s error about it. Teach the knowledge, and teach students to use it.

True or false?

A student can turn in excellent work made with AI and still have learned less than a classmate who worked without it.

Right That is the Bastani finding: better practice, worse exam. Assisted work and independent capability are two different things, so check them separately.

Not quite In the Bastani trial, students with unrestricted AI did better on practice and worse on the exam without it. The product hid the missing learning.

Difference read as a ceiling

Chapter 4 is about the differences students bring before they walk in: culture, language, income, gender. Each one can be read as an asset or as a ceiling. Teachers often pick the ceiling without noticing.

Language. In Week 3 you met BICS and CALP: everyday language comes in a year or two, academic language takes five to seven. A student still learning academic English may reason at a high level in another language. English learner status describes a service the school provides. It says nothing about the student’s ability.

Culture. Students come with ways of talking, working and showing respect that school may or may not reward. Culturally responsive teaching (Week 12) builds on what students bring.

Income. Chapter 4 shows that family income predicts achievement. Read that as opportunity. Children from low-income families get fewer books at home, fewer summer programs, and schools with fewer experienced teachers. Ziegler and Baker (2013) call these resources educational capital and learning capital. They are unequally distributed, and they shape what a test later reports as ability.

Your district file shows another kind of capital. Tanya’s parents are teachers. Her grade 3 referral is two pages long and names the subtests she should get. Knowing what to ask for is capital too.

Read the FRL column with care. Free and reduced lunch counts one thing: household income in this country, this year. It doesn’t count the parents’ schooling, their profession, or what they built somewhere else. A family can qualify honestly and still carry a great deal of educational capital. A teacher who reads “FRL, ELL” as “poor, uneducated, behind” has read three things the file never said.

True or false?

A gap in average test scores between high- and low-income students shows a gap in ability between the two groups.

Not quite The gap follows unequal opportunity: books, programs, experienced teachers, time. Chapter 4 reads achievement gaps as opportunity gaps.

Right A test measures what a student has learned so far, and learning depends on opportunity. Unequal resources produce unequal scores.

Learners with exceptionalities

A student is exceptional when the regular program does not meet their needs, because of a disability, a gift or talent, or both. In 2022–23, about 7.5 million U.S. students, 15% of public school students, received services under federal disability law. The largest group, 32% of them, had a specific learning disability (National Center for Education Statistics [NCES], 2024).

IDEA The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) guarantees every student with a qualifying disability a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment: as close to the regular classroom as their needs allow. Each student served gets an Individualized Education Program (IEP): goals, services and accommodations, written by a team that includes the parents.

Section 504 A civil rights law. It covers students whose disability limits a major life activity but who do not need special education. A 504 plan lists accommodations, such as extra time or a quiet testing room. It adds no specialized instruction.

Specific learning disability A difficulty in one area of learning, such as reading, writing or math, in a student whose general intelligence is typical or higher. Dyslexia is the most common: trouble decoding written words, rooted in processing the sounds of language (Lyon et al., 2003). It says nothing about how well the student thinks.

ADHD and autism ADHD shows as trouble sustaining attention, impulsivity, or hyperactivity. Autism shows as differences in social communication and repetitive behaviors or focused interests. Both vary widely, and many students with either diagnosis are capable of advanced work.

Intellectual disability Significant limits in both intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior (everyday conceptual, social and practical skills), beginning before age 22 (American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities [AAIDD], 2021). The AAIDD adds that limitations often coexist with strengths.

How students get identified. Most schools now use response to intervention (RTI), part of a wider system called MTSS. Everyone gets good instruction and a universal screening. Students who fall behind get extra help in small groups. Those who still don’t respond get more intensive help, and possibly a referral for evaluation.

A test in the wrong language. IDEA gives the U.S. one of the most thorough systems in the world for finding disabilities. Every child has a legal right to a free evaluation, and the school has to look. Many countries promise much less. A test, though, works only for the kind of students it was normed on. Most U.S. tests were normed mostly on children who grew up here speaking English. Give one to a student born abroad and a vocabulary or reading score can measure time in this country more than ability. The testing profession’s own standards call this a fairness problem (American Educational Research Association [AERA] et al., 2014). IDEA requires evaluation in the child’s native language, with tests that don’t discriminate. Schools still miss in both directions: English learners tend to be under-identified in the early grades and over-identified later (Samson & Lesaux, 2009; Sullivan, 2011).

A low score from a student born abroad is a question, and three checks answer most of it. Was the test given in a language the student fully commands? Were students like this one in the norm sample? Does the same difficulty show up in the student’s first language?

On paper, need decides who is evaluated. In your district file, a parent’s request decided it twice. The screening tool learned from those records. Ask the case’s fourth question again: what has the tool learned to predict?

Check yourself

Theo has ADHD. He needs extra time on tests and a seat away from the door. He does not need specialized instruction. Which plan fits?

Not every one An IEP comes with special education services. Theo needs accommodations only.

Risky Without a plan, his accommodations depend on which teacher he gets. A 504 plan makes them his right.

Yes Accommodations, no specialized instruction: that is what a 504 plan is for.

The opposite The least restrictive environment for Theo is the regular classroom with two accommodations.

The misconception: “dumb it down”

Ask a room of new teachers what to do for a student with a disability. Most say some version of make it easier. Shorter readings. Fewer questions. A video in place of the chapter. It comes from a kind place.

It is the most common mistake in this chapter, and it has a name in the law. An accommodation changes how a student gets to the learning or shows it. A modification changes what the student is expected to learn. Accommodations keep the bar where it is. Modifications lower it. Some students with significant disabilities need modifications. Most students with learning disabilities need accommodations.

Take Tanya. She has dyslexia and real talent in math. Her history class assigns a chapter a week. Two plans:

  • Plan A. Give her a video instead of the chapter. It feels kind. She gets a summary, and she reads less every week than her classmates. Over a year, the gap in reading grows.
  • Plan B. Pair text-to-speech with the reading. The tool reads the chapter aloud while Tanya follows the words on the page. She gets the same chapter, the same questions and extra time.

Plan B has evidence behind it. A meta-analysis of 22 studies found that text-to-speech improves reading comprehension for students with reading disabilities, a small-to-moderate effect, d = 0.35 (Wood et al., 2018). Her eyes stay on print, so she keeps practicing.

The accommodation is half the plan. Tanya also needs an intervention: direct, systematic teaching of how letters map to sounds, in a separate block, from a trained specialist (National Reading Panel, 2000). The accommodation gives her the history today. The intervention builds her decoding for tomorrow. And her math talent needs the third piece: work at her level, which may be well ahead of grade.

Why the bar matters for motivation. You learned this in Weeks 11 and 12. Self-efficacy grows from mastery experiences, and a success on an easy task teaches nothing about your ability. A student handed an easier task also reads the message: my teacher doesn’t expect much from me. That is the Mr. Hale problem from Week 12 again. Lowering the bar costs the student challenge, opportunity and belief, all at once.

Commit first

Ms. Grant teaches 8th-grade science. Her new student, Eli, has dyslexia. Her plan for him: readings rewritten at a 4th-grade level, no written lab reports, and videos for every chapter. She says, “I don’t want him to feel overwhelmed.”

What does each part of her plan cost Eli? Rewrite one part so it lowers the barrier and keeps the bar. Two or three sentences.

All three parts lower the bar. The 4th-grade readings cut the science vocabulary he needs. Dropping lab reports removes the practice of writing up evidence, which every scientist does. Videos in place of chapters stop his reading practice altogether. He will feel less overwhelmed this month, and fall further behind every month after.

One rewrite: grade-level readings with text-to-speech, so he hears the words while he reads them. Or: the lab report stays, and he can dictate it with speech-to-text, then edit. Same science, same report, a new route in. And ask whether Eli is getting decoding intervention somewhere in his week.

Universal Design for Learning

Accommodations fix the lesson for one student after the fact. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) builds options in from the start, for everyone (CAST, 2024). The idea comes from architecture. A ramp built for wheelchair users also helps parents with strollers and workers with carts. Captions written for deaf viewers help everyone in a loud room.

UDL has three principles:

Engagement Offer more than one way in. Choice of topic, relevance to students’ lives, a manageable level of challenge, and feedback that helps them persist.

Representation Offer the content more than one way. Text with audio, a diagram with a description, a key word with its meaning. Every student gets the same content.

Action and expression Offer more than one way to show learning. Writing, speaking, building, drawing, recording. The goal stays fixed. The route is flexible.

UDL is not learning styles. Learning styles sort students into types and match the format. UDL gives everyone the options and lets students use what removes their barrier today. The UDL motto: firm goals, flexible means.

True or false?

Under UDL, a teacher first diagnoses each student’s learning style, then gives each student the format that matches it.

Not quite That is the learning-styles claim, which fails when tested. UDL offers options to everyone and keeps the goal the same for all.

Right UDL plans for the whole range of students at once. No diagnosis, no sorting: options built in, one goal.

AI that restores capability

Some of the most important AI in your students’ lives was built for disability. Each of these tools lowers a barrier. None of them lowers the bar.

  • Seeing for blind users. Be My Eyes added Be My AI in 2023. A blind user takes a photo, and the app describes it aloud and answers follow-up questions (Be My Eyes, 2023).
  • Speaking again. A man with ALS who could no longer speak clearly received a brain implant. The system turned his attempted speech into words with about 97% accuracy, in a voice built from old recordings of his own (Card et al., 2024).
  • Keeping your own voice. Apple’s Personal Voice, released in 2023, lets a person at risk of losing speech record about 15 minutes of their voice. The phone then speaks typed text in that voice (Apple, 2023).
  • Sign language to text. Google announced SignGemma in 2025, an AI model that translates American Sign Language into English text (Google DeepMind, 2025).
  • Reading and writing. Text-to-speech, speech-to-text and live captions are built into every phone and laptop your students carry.

Here is the hard part for a teacher. The same tool can restore access or offload the learning. Text-to-speech on a history chapter gives Tanya the history. Text-to-speech on a decoding lesson removes the very practice the lesson exists for. Speech-to-text on a lab report gives Eli the science. Speech-to-text on a spelling test skips the spelling.

Ask one question every time: is the tool doing the thing this lesson is for? If it is, it offloads the learning. If it removes a barrier around the learning, it is an accommodation, and often augmentation.

Check yourself

Owen is blind. Which use of AI offloads what the lesson is for?

Access The lesson is about persuasion. Hearing the article removes a barrier and leaves the persuading to him.

Access The lesson is the history. The description gives him what sighted classmates see.

Access Dictation changes the route. He still builds the argument and revises it.

Yes The lesson is writing a persuasive essay, and the tool did it. Slow typing is a real barrier, and dictation fixes it without taking the thinking.

Twice-exceptional: both at once

A twice-exceptional (2e) student has a gift or talent and a disability at the same time. Reis et al. (2014) define 2e students as those whose high ability and disability both need attention, together, in the same plan.

The problem is masking. The strength hides the disability, the disability hides the strength, or each hides the other.

Look at the chart. A student who reasons at 132 and decodes at 78 can average to 106. On a single total score, she looks typical. No gifted referral, because she isn’t high enough. No disability referral, because she isn’t low enough. Teachers see a bright kid who “doesn’t try” on reading.

There are three common patterns (Baum et al., 2017):

  1. The gift shows, the disability hides. A bright student compensates for years, until the reading load outgrows the workarounds. Often in middle school.
  2. The disability shows, the gift hides. The student is served for the disability only. Nobody offers the advanced work.
  3. Each hides the other. The student looks average and is served for neither.

What 2e students need is both, at the same time. Strength-based plans start with the talent: advanced work in the strong domain, plus accommodations and intervention for the disability. A plan that “fixes the reading first, then we’ll see about math” often loses the student’s motivation before the math ever comes. Tanya’s plan only works because it serves both.

In our paper, Desmet and I warn about AI here (Parra-Martinez & Desmet, 2026). A system that receives a disability label and quietly lowers expectations along every dimension at once has repeated, at scale, the mistake 2e research has documented for two decades.

Check yourself

Nia’s IEP is for a writing disability. In class discussion she makes connections nobody else in the room makes. Her written work is short and messy. What fits best?

Fix-first Waiting for the weakness to close before serving the strength is the pattern that loses 2e students. Serve both now.

Yes Strength and disability, at the same time. Advanced discussion work feeds the talent. Speech-to-text or a scribe lets her show what she knows.

Masking A strength in one area doesn’t cancel a disability in another. That is exactly how 2e students get missed.

Lowers the bar Easy tasks don’t build self-efficacy. They tell her what you expect of her.

Commit first

Go back to the district file. Michael B. was never evaluated. The screening tool flagged him for a sustained grade decline. You have read about him all term: he tried hard early, failed a major assignment, and now says, “Why bother? I’m not good at this subject.”

Name two things you would want to know about Michael before anyone writes a plan for him. For each, say why it matters. Two or three sentences.

There is no single right answer yet. Good questions look at what the record leaves out:

  • What kind of work does he fail, and what kind does he manage? Reading-heavy work, or all work? A pattern across task types tells you more than a grade.
  • Was he ever screened for reading, and who would have asked? The file shows evaluations happen when someone knows to ask.
  • What is he good at? An asset-based plan starts there.

Keep your two questions. We will come back to Michael.

Bring it to class

Four questions close the case. In person: bring your answers Tuesday, and bring the file; we add to it. Online: think them through this week, and use them in Discussion 1.

  1. Who in this class has been evaluated, and who asked for it?
  2. What had to go right for Tanya’s evaluation, and did each of those things happen for Matthew?
  3. Is Tanya the only student the 2e description could fit?
  4. If the referral process depended on parents knowing what to ask for, what has the screening tool learned to predict?

Lower the barrier. Keep the bar. Then look again, because the student who needs you most may be the one nobody asked about.
